desc:
You may insert any lowercase letters at any positions of the string s (letters of s are never removed or reordered). Make s a palindrome using the fewest insertions. Among all palindromes of that minimum length, return the lexicographically smallest one.

In other words, return the lexicographically smallest among the shortest palindromes that contain s as a subsequence.

For example, "ab" gives "aba" ("bab" also has length 3 but is larger). "abc" gives "abcba". "ba" gives "aba". "zzz" is already a palindrome and gives "zzz".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: First think about how to find just the minimum number of insertions for s[i..j] by looking at the two end letters.

Let best(i, j) be the smallest shortest palindrome containing s[i..j] as a subsequence. If s[i] == s[j], wrap those letters around best(i+1, j-1). Otherwise one of the end letters needs a new mirror copy.

If s[i] != s[j], the candidates are s[i] + best(i+1, j) + s[i] and s[j] + best(i, j-1) + s[j]. Take the shorter one, and the lexicographically smaller one when the lengths tie. Build the table by increasing interval length and store the strings themselves.
editorial: The length part is the classic palindrome-insertion DP: if the end letters are equal they pair with each other, otherwise one of them is mirrored by an inserted copy. The same recurrence can carry the actual strings. For an interval [i, j] store best(i, j), the lexicographically smallest among the shortest palindromic supersequences of s[i..j].

Equal end letters: best(i, j) = s[i] + best(i+1, j-1) + s[i]. This is optimal even among palindromes that do not pair the two ends, because any shortest palindrome for the interval starts with s[i], and what lies between its outer letters must be a shortest palindromic supersequence of the inner interval, from which the smallest is chosen. For a fixed outer letter, a smaller inner part gives a smaller whole string, so greedy choice of the inner minimum is valid.

Different end letters: any shortest palindrome starts with s[i] or s[j], since a different first letter would be an extra pair that helps neither end. So compare the two candidates s[i] + best(i+1, j) + s[i] and s[j] + best(i, j-1) + s[j] by (length, then lexicographic order). Only the two previous interval lengths are needed at a time. There are O(n2) intervals and each builds a string of length O(n), so the time is O(n3) (with very fast string concatenation) and the space is O(n2) characters.
